exercises.prompt: Which line opens `$path` for reading in the way this lesson recommends?

options.label: `open my $fh, '<', $path or die "Cannot read $path: $!";`
options.feedback: Yes: three arguments, a lexical handle, a loose-binding `or`, and a message with the path and the reason in `$!`.

options.label: `open my $fh, '<', $path || die "Cannot read $path: $!";`
options.feedback: Not yet. `||` binds tightly, so this means `$path || die ...`; since `$path` is true, `die` never runs, even when `open` fails.

options.label: `open FH, $path;`
options.feedback: Not yet. This is the old two-argument form with a global handle and no error check; a filename starting with `>` would even be opened for writing.

options.label: `open my $fh, '>', $path or die "Cannot read $path: $!";`
options.feedback: Not yet. `'>'` opens for *writing* and empties the file first: a costly mistake when you meant to read.

hints: Look at the mode, the operator before `die`, and the number of arguments.
exercises.solution: Use the three-argument `open` with a lexical handle, `'<'` for reading, and `or die` with a message that includes the path and `$!`. Option (b) never dies because of precedence, (c) is the unsafe two-argument form with no check, and (d) truncates the file.

feedback.message: Not yet. When the message does not end in a newline, `die` appends the file and line number.

hints: One message ends with `\n` and the other does not.
What does `die` add to a message without a trailing newline?
exercises.solution: `die "first\n"` uses the message as it is, so `$@` contains no line number: `plain`. `die "second"` has no trailing newline, so Perl appends ` at main.pl line N.`, which the pattern finds: `located`. The output is `plain located`.

feedback.message: Not yet. Division by zero dies inside the `eval`, so the `or do` block runs and appends `X`.

hints: What happens when Perl divides by zero?
The `or do` block runs only when the `eval` returns false.
exercises.solution: 12 / 4 is 3, so the `eval` returns 1 and the log becomes `3,`. 12 / 0 dies with `Illegal division by zero`, so the `eval` returns false and `or do` appends `X`. 12 / 2 is 6. Each pass adds a comma: `3,X,6,`.

feedback.message: Not yet. `$.` is the number of the line just read, counting from 1, and the loop stops right after reading `delta`.

hints: `$.` counts the lines read so far from the last handle read.
exercises.solution: The loop reads `alpha`, `beta`, `gamma` and then `delta`, which starts with `d`, so `last` leaves the loop. `$.` is the number of the line just read: 4.

feedback.message: Not yet. That is the number of UTF-8 *bytes*. `use utf8` makes the string literal a string of characters.

hints: `use utf8` tells Perl that string literals in the source are UTF-8 text.
Count the characters, including the space.
exercises.solution: With `use utf8`, the literal is decoded into characters: n, a, ï, v, e, space, c, a, f, é. That is 10. Without `use utf8`, Perl would see the UTF-8 bytes, and `ï` and `é` take two bytes each, giving 12.

hints: `die` was given a hash reference, so that is what `$@` holds.
`eval` returns undef when the block dies, so `//` supplies a fallback.
exercises.solution: `check(-5)` dies with a hash reference. `eval` catches it, returns undef, and stores the reference in `$@`. `// 'failed'` turns the undef into `failed`. `ref($@)` is `HASH`, and `$@->{field}` is `qty`. Output: `HASH qty failed`.

exercises.prompt: A nightly script rewrites `prices.csv`, which a web server reads at any moment. Why do careful scripts write to a temporary file in the same directory and then `rename` it over `prices.csv`?

options.label: Because the rename replaces the file in one step, readers see either the whole old file or the whole new one, never a half-written file
options.feedback: Yes. On Unix, renaming within one file system is atomic, so there is no moment when the file is incomplete.

options.label: Because writing directly to an existing file is not allowed in Perl
options.feedback: Not yet. Opening with `'>'` works fine; the problem is what readers see while the write is in progress.

options.label: Because `rename` compresses the file
options.feedback: Not yet. `rename` changes only the name (the directory entry), not the contents.

options.label: Because temporary files are faster to write to
options.feedback: Not yet. Speed is the same; the point is atomic replacement.

hints: Think about a reader that opens the file while the script is half-way through writing.
Which operation happens in one indivisible step?
exercises.solution: Writing in place leaves a window during which the file is truncated or half-written, and a crash in that window leaves it broken. Writing to a temporary file and then renaming means the switch from old to new happens in a single atomic step, and a crash before the rename leaves the old file intact. The temporary file must be in the same directory (the same file system) for the rename to be atomic.
